How many universities are there in Denmark, and how long do a bachelor's and a master's degree take?
Eight universities. Bachelor's about three years, master's (kandidat) about two years.
What does SU stand for?
Statens Uddannelsesstøtte (the State Education Grant) – financial support from the state to students.
What is a diploma programme (diplomuddannelse)?
A part-time higher education at bachelor level, typically 2–3 years. You pay for it yourself.
What does AMU stand for?
Labour market training (arbejdsmarkedsuddannelser) – short courses, mainly for skilled and unskilled workers.
What is FVU, and where do you take it?
Courses for adults who have problems with spelling, reading or maths. Taken at VUC. Normally from age 25.
What is OBU?
Dyslexia teaching for adults at VUC. Normally from age 25.
What is avu?
General adult education at VUC – single subjects at primary/lower secondary level. The highest level is D. Normally from age 25.
What does VUC stand for?
Adult education centres (Voksenuddannelsescentre).
Who is responsible for day care in Denmark?
The municipalities.
Do all children have the right to a place in day care?
Yes.
Who pays for day care?
The municipality pays part, the parents pay the rest. With a low income or as a single parent you can apply for a subsidy.
Why, since the 1960s, did people want children looked after outside the home?
To get women into the labour market.
Which age group is a nursery (vuggestue) for?
Children from about six months up to about three years.
What is dagpleje (childminding)?
Children are looked after by a childminder together with two to four other children in the childminder's private home (approx. 6 months – 3 years).
Which age group is a kindergarten (børnehave) for?
Children from about three up to six years.
What does SFO stand for?
School after-school scheme (SkoleFritidsOrdning) – looks after folkeskole children before and after school hours.
Who are clubs (klubtilbud) for?
Older children and young people, after school.
Who elects the parents' board, and what does it have influence on?
The parents elect representatives. The board has influence on the institution's finances and activities.
May you smoke in a childminder's home?
Not in the parts where the children stay.
Who decides most rules about employment conditions in Denmark?
The labour market parties – the trade unions and the employers' organisations (not the Folketing). The system goes back to 1899.
An agreement between trade unions and employers' organisations about pay, working hours, etc. Usually lasts two or three years.
What is the peace obligation (fredspligt)?
No strikes or lockouts as long as the collective agreement applies.
What is a strike?
Employees stop working until a collective agreement has been reached.
What is a lockout?
The employer bars union members from coming to work until a collective agreement has been reached.
Which bodies decide on breaches of collective agreements?
The Labour Court (Arbejdsretten) and industrial arbitration tribunals (outside the ordinary courts).
What is the system called where the labour market parties, not the Folketing, decide labour market conditions?
The Danish model.
What is flexicurity?
Easy for employers to hire and fire (flexibility) – in return employees are financially secured through unemployment benefits (security).
Is there a statutory minimum wage in Denmark?
No. It depends on the collective agreements.
What is set by law (and not by collective agreement) regarding holidays?
Five weeks' holiday is set by law.
Which strike did the Folketing stop in 2021?
The nurses' strike (after more than two months) – the Folketing imposed the agreement by law.
Which groups are often not covered by collective agreements?
Many highly educated people in the private sector (engineers, economists, lawyers), the restaurant industry and traditionally agriculture.
What share of employees are members of a trade union today?
About two out of three (68 percent). In 1990 it was about five out of six.
Is it a requirement to be a member of a trade union?
No, it is voluntary. No one may force you to be a member.
May an employer fire a person because they join or leave a trade union?
No.
Which occupational groups does HK represent?
Trade and office: shop staff, laboratory technicians, secretaries, receptionists, dental/clinic assistants.
Which occupational groups does FOA represent?
Home care, social and healthcare assistants (SOSU), firefighters, canteen staff.
Which occupational groups does 3F represent?
Industry, transport and construction: welders, drivers, bricklayers, carpenters, cleaners and other unskilled workers.
Who elects the shop steward, and how many employees must there typically be?
The union members at the workplace elect them – typically at workplaces with more than ten employees. The employer does not attend the meeting.
What is the shop steward's job?
To represent the employees towards management (e.g. in pay negotiations) and give advice. Has special protection against dismissal.
What are the union's meetings at the workplace called?
Club meetings (klubmøder).
What is the work environment representative's job?
To keep an eye on the physical and psychological work environment (e.g. safety equipment, support, bullying, stress).
Who must get an employment contract (ansættelsesbevis), and when?
Everyone who works more than three hours a week for more than four weeks – no later than one month after starting.
What may an employer not ask about in a job interview?
Health (unrelated to the job), sick days in previous jobs, pregnancy/plans for children and religion.
What is the most common working time per week?
37 hours.
Can the employer demand that you go part-time?
No. You can ask for reduced hours, but the employer decides whether you get it.
How many holiday days do you earn per month, and how many weeks of holiday do you get per year?
About two holiday days per month – five weeks of paid holiday after a full year. Some have a sixth week.
When do you normally have the right to three consecutive weeks of holiday?
Between 1 May and 30 September.
A committee at larger workplaces where management and the employees' shop stewards discuss conditions.
What do the rules on dismissal require of the employer in most cases?
A fair and genuine reason (e.g. unsuitability, cooperation problems or cutbacks).
For what reasons may an employer not dismiss an employee?
Gender, race, skin colour, religion, political views, sexual orientation, age, disability, national/social/ethnic origin, pregnancy or maternity leave.
What is an a-kasse?
An unemployment insurance fund – a voluntary insurance (members' association) that pays unemployment benefits (dagpenge). Supported by the state.
What must you do to get unemployment benefits?
Have worked beforehand, be available for the labour market, actively look for work, accept offered work and take part in meetings and activities.
What is the digital job plan for the unemployed called?
"Min Plan" (My Plan).
When does the municipality take over responsibility for an unemployed a-kasse member?
After four months of unemployment.
What can you get if you lose your job and are not a member of an a-kasse?
Social assistance (kontanthjælp) from the municipality (depends on your own and your spouse's income and assets). Normally lower than unemployment benefits.
Where do you register as self-employed?
With the Danish Business Authority (Erhvervsstyrelsen), via its website.
What duty does a self-employed person have?
To keep accounts and report the business's profit or loss to SKAT (the tax authority).
Roughly how many full-time farmers are there in Denmark today?
About 10,000 (compared with almost 200,000 before 1960).
What share of farmland is farmed organically?
About 11 percent.
What is a cooperative (andelsselskab), and how many votes does each farmer have?
A company owned by the farmers themselves. Each farmer has one vote, no matter how much he supplies.
What are the two big cooperatives for dairies and slaughterhouses called?
Arla (dairy) and Danish Crown (slaughterhouse).
Which countries do Arla's owners come from?
Denmark, Sweden, Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg and the UK (almost 10,000 farmers).
Which company is known for building bricks?
LEGO.
Which Danish pharmaceutical company produces insulin, among other things?
Novo Nordisk.
What share of the world's hearing aids are made in Denmark?
Over a third.
What is the world's largest wind turbine manufacturer (2024), and where is it based?
Vestas – in Denmark.
Which wind turbine from 1957 inspired the modern wind turbine industry?
The Gedser turbine (and the Tvind turbine 1975–78).
What do Rockwool, Grundfos, Danfoss and Velux produce?
Rockwool = insulation; Grundfos = pumps; Danfoss = thermostats; Velux = windows.
Which country does Denmark import most from, and which country does it export most to?
Imports most from Germany; exports most to the USA.
Who are Denmark's two biggest trading partners in 2025?
The USA (14.1%) and Germany (12.7%). Then Sweden, the Netherlands, the UK, China, Norway.
What is Mærsk?
A Danish shipping company – one of the world's two biggest container shipping lines.
When is Danish oil production planned to have stopped completely?
What is ISS?
A Danish service company (cleaning, property services, security) with about half a million employees worldwide.
What is the principle of the Danish welfare society?
Everyone who can contributes (works and pays tax), and everyone in need can get help from the public sector.
Who pays for welfare?
Citizens through taxes, VAT and duties – plus corporate taxes, property taxes and returns on pension savings.
What is the principle of taxation in Denmark?
The more you earn, the larger the share of your pay you pay in tax.
How high is VAT (moms) in Denmark?
25 percent.
What is the child benefit (børnechecken)?
Child and youth benefit paid to parents of children under 18. High earners get less or nothing.
What is financial help during longer illness called?
Sickness benefit (sygedagpenge).
What is a flex job (fleksjob)?
You work and earn part of your income yourself and get the rest as a public benefit – for people with reduced working capacity.
Who can get early retirement pension (førtidspension)?
People with a permanent and substantially reduced ability to work.
From what age can you get the state pension (folkepension) in 2026?
From 67 (the age limit is gradually being raised).
What is the residence requirement for the state pension and early retirement pension?
Danish citizenship (as a main rule), permanent residence in Denmark and at least three years' residence after turning 15.
How long must you have lived in Denmark to get the full state pension?
40 years. If you have lived here for a shorter time, you get a pension in proportion to the number of years.
What is a labour market pension (arbejdsmarkedspension)?
A pension paid in through your job – on top of the state pension.
Help with rent for tenants with low income. Pensioners with low income can often get higher housing benefit.
What is the health insurance card commonly called?
"The yellow card" (det gule kort). Everyone registered in the CPR gets one.
What does health insurance group 1 (sikringsgruppe 1) mean?
You are registered with a specific GP and need a referral to a specialist (except ear and eye doctors) for free treatment.
What does it cost to borrow books at the library?
It is free.
Which two bridges cost money to drive across?
The Øresund Bridge and the Great Belt Bridge (Storebæltsbroen).
What are duties (afgifter), and why do we have them?
Special taxes on e.g. cars, petrol, alcohol, cigarettes, batteries, disposable tableware and carrier bags – justified by revenue, environment and health.
What is the minimum age for getting married?
18 years.
May you be married to several people at once?
No – only one at a time.
May you force someone to get married?
No. Both parties must want the marriage.
Can same-sex couples marry and adopt children?
Yes, on an equal footing with other couples.
Where can you get married?
At the town hall, in the Church of Denmark or in recognised religious communities (the priest/leader must be authorised for the wedding to be valid).
What does joint custody mean?
That the parents together make important decisions about the child (name, upbringing, school, religion, childcare).
How do unmarried parents get joint custody?
By making a declaration in connection with the birth that they will share the care and responsibility.
What share of marriages end in divorce?
About 40 percent.
What is separation?
A kind of trial period where you are still married but normally live apart.
When are you entitled to a divorce after separation?
After six months of separation. If you agree, you can divorce straight away.
Who helps parents who cannot agree about the children after a divorce?
